Aql.name: Aquila
Aql.find: Find bright Altair, the southern corner of the Summer Triangle, with a fainter star on each side.
Aql.myth: The eagle that carried thunderbolts for the king of the Greek gods.

And.name: Andromeda
And.find: Follow the line of stars running northeast from the top-left corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.
And.myth: A princess chained to a sea rock as a sacrifice, until Perseus arrived and freed her.

Scl.name: Sculptor
Scl.find: A faint area south of Cetus, near Fomalhaut.

Ara.name: Ara
Ara.myth: The altar where the Greek gods swore loyalty before their war with the Titans.

Lib.name: Libra
Lib.find: Between Spica and Scorpius; its two main stars form the beam of a balance.
Lib.myth: Scales of justice; the stars were once seen as the claws of the Scorpion.

Cet.name: Cetus
Cet.find: A big, sprawling pattern below Aries and Pisces; its 'tail' star Diphda is the brightest.
Cet.myth: The sea monster sent to devour Andromeda, which Perseus turned to stone.

Ari.name: Aries
Ari.find: A short bent line of three stars between the Pleiades and the Great Square of Pegasus.
Ari.myth: The ram with the golden fleece that later sent Jason and the Argonauts on their quest.

Sct.name: Scutum
Sct.find: A small group in a bright Milky Way patch below Aquila.
Sct.myth: No myth: Hevelius named it after the shield of a Polish king.

Pyx.name: Pyxis
Pyx.find: A small faint line of stars next to Puppis.
Pyx.myth: No myth: Lacaille's ship's compass, added to the old ship Argo.

Boo.name: Bootes
Boo.find: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle to orange Arcturus; the constellation looks like a kite.
Boo.myth: A herdsman forever chasing the two bears around the pole.

Cae.name: Caelum
Cae.find: A faint pair of stars between Columba and Eridanus.
Cae.myth: No myth: Lacaille named it after an engraver's chisel.

Cha.name: Chamaeleon
Cha.find: A small faint group close to the south celestial pole.
Cha.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Cnc.name: Cancer
Cnc.find: A faint upside-down Y between Gemini and Leo; look for the misty Beehive Cluster at its centre.
Cnc.myth: A crab sent to distract Hercules in his fight with the Hydra; he crushed it underfoot.

Cap.name: Capricornus
Cap.find: A wide, faint triangle of stars southwest of Aquarius.
Cap.myth: A creature with a goat's front and a fish's tail, linked to a god who escaped a monster by leaping into a river.

Car.name: Carina
Car.find: Bright Canopus marks it, well south of Sirius; best from the southern hemisphere.
Car.myth: The keel of the Argonauts' ship Argo, which was split into three constellations in the 1700s.

Cas.name: Cassiopeia
Cas.find: A bright W or M shape on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper.
Cas.myth: A vain queen who boasted about her beauty and was placed in the sky, sometimes upside down, as punishment.

Cen.name: Centaurus
Cen.find: A large southern pattern whose two bright 'pointer' stars lead to the Southern Cross.
Cen.myth: A wise centaur who taught many Greek heroes.

Cep.name: Cepheus
Cep.find: A house shape with a pointed roof, between Cassiopeia and the Little Dipper.
Cep.myth: The king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda.

Com.name: Coma Berenices
Com.find: A faint spray of stars between Leo's tail and Boötes; it looks like a loose cluster.
Com.myth: A queen who cut off her hair as an offering for her husband's safe return from war.

CVn.name: Canes Venatici
CVn.find: Just below the Big Dipper's handle; the brightest star is Cor Caroli.
CVn.myth: The two dogs held on a leash by Boötes the herdsman.

Aur.name: Auriga
Aur.find: Brilliant yellow Capella marks a lopsided pentagon of stars high above Orion in winter.
Aur.myth: A charioteer said to have invented the four-horse chariot, often drawn holding a goat and her kids.

Col.name: Columba
Col.find: South of Lepus, below Orion's feet.
Col.myth: Sometimes linked to the dove Noah released from the ark; named around 1592.

Cir.name: Circinus
Cir.find: A tiny group next to Alpha Centauri.

Crt.name: Crater
Crt.find: A faint cup shape next to Corvus, sitting on Hydra's back.
Crt.myth: The cup that the crow was sent to fill with water.

CrA.name: Corona Australis
CrA.find: A small curved arc of stars below the Teapot of Sagittarius.
CrA.myth: A wreath of leaves, sometimes said to have been placed there by the god of wine.

CrB.name: Corona Borealis
CrB.find: A small, neat semicircle of stars between Arcturus and Vega.
CrB.myth: The jewelled crown given to Ariadne at her wedding.

Crv.name: Corvus
Crv.find: A small, bright four-sided shape southwest of Spica.
Crv.myth: A crow punished for lying to Apollo, and placed forever just out of reach of the water cup, Crater.

Cru.name: Crux
Cru.find: The smallest constellation: a bright kite-shaped cross next to the Centaur's two pointer stars.
Cru.myth: Known for thousands of years to southern peoples; it guided sailors and appears on several national flags.

Cyg.name: Cygnus
Cyg.find: A large cross shape along the Milky Way; Deneb at the top is one corner of the Summer Triangle.
Cyg.myth: A god who took the form of a swan; also said to be a friend mourning Phaethon by the river.

Del.name: Delphinus
Del.find: A small diamond with a short tail, just east of Altair.
Del.myth: The dolphin that persuaded a sea nymph to marry Poseidon.

Dor.name: Dorado
Dor.find: Far south; it contains part of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
Dor.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Dra.name: Draco
Dra.find: A long winding line of stars that curls between the Big and Little Dippers.
Dra.myth: The dragon that guarded the golden apples, defeated by Hercules.

Nor.name: Norma
Nor.find: A faint group in the Milky Way between Lupus and Ara.

Eri.name: Eridanus
Eri.find: A long chain of faint stars winding south from near Rigel to bright Achernar.
Eri.myth: The river into which Phaethon fell after losing control of the Sun's chariot.

Sge.name: Sagitta
Sge.find: A small, clear arrow shape inside the Summer Triangle.
Sge.myth: An arrow fired by Hercules, or by the god of love.

For.name: Fornax
For.find: A dim area inside the bend of Eridanus.

Gem.name: Gemini
Gem.find: Two bright stars side by side, Castor and Pollux, above and to the left of Orion.
Gem.myth: Twin brothers, one mortal and one immortal, who chose to share their fate.

Cam.name: Camelopardalis
Cam.find: A large, dim area between Polaris and Capella; you need a dark sky.
Cam.myth: No myth: added around 1612 by Petrus Plancius.

CMa.name: Canis Major
CMa.find: Follow Orion's belt down and to the left to Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.
CMa.myth: Orion's larger hunting dog, following him across the sky.

UMa.name: Ursa Major
UMa.find: Its seven brightest stars make the Big Dipper, or Plough.
UMa.myth: A nymph turned into a bear and placed in the sky, circling the pole forever.

Gru.name: Grus
Gru.find: A long-necked bird shape south of Piscis Austrinus and its star Fomalhaut.
Gru.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Her.name: Hercules
Her.find: Between Vega and Arcturus, look for the 'Keystone', a four-star box.
Her.myth: The strongest of the Greek heroes, famous for his twelve labours.

Hor.name: Horologium
Hor.find: A faint line of stars near Achernar.

Hya.name: Hydra
Hya.find: The largest constellation: its small head of stars lies below Cancer and its body stretches far to the east.
Hya.myth: The many-headed serpent that Hercules fought.

Hyi.name: Hydrus
Hyi.find: Between the two Magellanic Clouds, far south.
Hyi.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Ind.name: Indus
Ind.find: A faint group south of Microscopium and Capricornus.
Ind.myth: No myth: named around the 1590s, possibly for the people met by Dutch explorers.

Lac.name: Lacerta
Lac.find: A small zigzag of faint stars between Cygnus and Cassiopeia.
Lac.myth: No myth: added by Johannes Hevelius in 1687.

Mon.name: Monoceros
Mon.find: A faint area inside the triangle formed by Betelgeuse, Sirius and Procyon.
Mon.myth: No myth: added around 1612 by Plancius.

Lep.name: Lepus
Lep.find: A small group directly below Orion's feet.
Lep.myth: A hare being chased by Orion and his dogs.

Leo.name: Leo
Leo.find: Look for a backwards question mark, the 'Sickle', ending at bright Regulus.
Leo.myth: The fierce lion with an unbreakable hide, defeated by Hercules.

Lup.name: Lupus
Lup.myth: A wild animal held by the Centaur; the Greeks saw it simply as a beast.

Lyn.name: Lynx
Lyn.find: A faint line of stars between the Big Dipper and Gemini.
Lyn.myth: No myth: Hevelius said you need the eyes of a lynx to see it.

Lyr.name: Lyra
Lyr.find: Brilliant Vega with a small parallelogram of stars beside it.
Lyr.myth: The lyre of Orpheus, whose music could charm even rocks and trees.

Ant.name: Antlia
Ant.find: A faint patch south of Hydra's long body, between Vela and Crater.
Ant.myth: No myth: it was added in the 1750s by Lacaille to honour a laboratory pump.

Mic.name: Microscopium
Mic.find: A faint area south of Capricornus.

Mus.name: Musca
Mus.find: A compact group just south of the Southern Cross.
Mus.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Oct.name: Octans
Oct.find: The constellation that holds the south celestial pole; its stars are faint.

Aps.name: Apus
Aps.find: Very far south, just below Triangulum Australe and close to the south celestial pole.
Aps.myth: No myth: Dutch sailors' star charts of the 1590s named it after the exotic birds of New Guinea.

Oph.name: Ophiuchus
Oph.find: A big coffin shape above Scorpius, between Hercules and the Scorpion.
Oph.myth: A healer so skilled he could bring back the dead, shown wrestling a huge snake.

Ori.name: Orion
Ori.find: Three bright stars in a row make Orion's belt, between red Betelgeuse and blue-white Rigel.
Ori.myth: A giant hunter placed opposite the Scorpion so they never share the sky.

Pav.name: Pavo
Pav.find: Bright Peacock star sits south of Sagittarius, near the south pole.
Pav.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Peg.name: Pegasus
Peg.find: Four stars form the large Great Square, high in the autumn sky.
Peg.myth: The winged horse that sprang from Medusa and carried heroes.

Pic.name: Pictor
Pic.find: A faint group next to bright Canopus.

Per.name: Perseus
Per.find: An arc of stars between Cassiopeia and the Pleiades; it includes the 'demon star' Algol.
Per.myth: The hero who beheaded Medusa and rescued Andromeda.

Equ.name: Equuleus
Equ.find: A small faint group between Delphinus and the Great Square of Pegasus.
Equ.myth: A foal sometimes said to be the brother of Pegasus.

CMi.name: Canis Minor
CMi.find: Bright Procyon and one fainter star, to the left of Orion and below Gemini.

LMi.name: Leo Minor
LMi.find: A few faint stars between Leo and the Big Dipper.
LMi.myth: No myth: added by Hevelius in 1687.

Vul.name: Vulpecula
Vul.find: Faint stars inside the Summer Triangle, just above the Arrow.
Vul.myth: No myth: added by Hevelius in 1687.

UMi.name: Ursa Minor
UMi.find: Polaris, the North Star, is the tip of the Little Dipper's handle; the Big Dipper's pointer stars lead to it.
UMi.myth: The son of the Great Bear, placed beside his mother.

Phe.name: Phoenix
Phe.find: A faint group near bright Achernar.
Phe.myth: No myth in Greek sky lore; named after the bird reborn from its own ashes.

Psc.name: Pisces
Psc.find: A large faint V shape around the Great Square, with a small 'circlet' of stars below Pegasus.
Psc.myth: Two fish tied together by a cord, said to be a goddess and her son escaping a monster.

PsA.name: Piscis Austrinus
PsA.find: Bright, lonely Fomalhaut in the autumn sky below Aquarius.
PsA.myth: A fish drinking the water poured by Aquarius.

Vol.name: Volans
Vol.find: A small group near Carina, far south.
Vol.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Pup.name: Puppis
Pup.find: Along the Milky Way, southeast of Sirius.
Pup.myth: The stern of the Argonauts' ship Argo.

Ret.name: Reticulum
Ret.find: A small diamond near the Large Magellanic Cloud.
Ret.myth: No myth: Lacaille named it after the crosshairs in a telescope eyepiece.

Sgr.name: Sagittarius
Sgr.find: Below the Milky Way's brightest part; its main stars form a 'Teapot'.
Sgr.myth: A centaur archer aiming his bow at the heart of the Scorpion.

Sco.name: Scorpius
Sco.find: A long curving J of stars with red Antares at its heart, low in the summer sky.
Sco.myth: The scorpion that killed Orion; the two now rise and set on opposite sides of the sky.

Ser.name: Serpens
Ser.find: Split in two by Ophiuchus: the head lies to the west and the tail to the east.
Ser.myth: The great snake held by the healer Ophiuchus.

Sex.name: Sextans
Sex.find: A faint area below Leo's Regulus.
Sex.myth: No myth: Hevelius named it after his own astronomical instrument.

Men.name: Mensa
Men.find: A very faint group near the south pole, partly covering the Large Magellanic Cloud.
Men.myth: No myth: Lacaille named it after the mountain above Cape Town.

Tau.name: Taurus
Tau.find: The orange star Aldebaran sits in a V-shaped face near the Pleiades, to the upper right of Orion.
Tau.myth: A god in the shape of a bull who carried a princess across the sea.

Tel.name: Telescopium
Tel.find: A faint area below the Southern Crown.

Tuc.name: Tucana
Tuc.find: Far south; it holds the Small Magellanic Cloud.
Tuc.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Tri.name: Triangulum
Tri.find: A small, narrow triangle between Aries and Andromeda.
Tri.myth: Linked by the Greeks to the shape of the Nile delta or of Sicily.

Tra.name: Triangulum Australe
Tra.find: A bright, neat triangle near Alpha Centauri.
Tra.myth: No myth: named on Dutch star charts of the 1590s.

Aqr.name: Aquarius
Aqr.find: Below Pegasus, look for a small Y-shaped group of four stars, the 'water jar'.
Aqr.myth: A young man pouring water from a jar; the Babylonians tied this region of sky to the rainy season.

Vir.name: Virgo
Vir.find: Follow the Big Dipper's handle through Arcturus and 'spike' down to Spica.
Vir.myth: A goddess of the harvest, often linked to the changing seasons.

Vel.name: Vela
Vel.find: Along the southern Milky Way; the 'False Cross' is shared with Carina.
Vel.myth: The sails of the Argonauts' ship Argo.

Sun.text: Our local star: a ball of hot gas about 109 times wider than Earth. It holds 99.8% of the Solar System's mass.
Sun.distance: 1 AU (about 150 million km); its light takes about 8.3 minutes to reach us
Sun.colour: white (it often looks yellow through our air)
Sun.fact: Never look at the Sun directly or through binoculars or a telescope without a proper solar filter.

Moon.text: Earth's only natural satellite, about a quarter of Earth's width. The same face always points towards us.
Moon.fact: Its dark patches, the 'seas', are old lava plains. Even small binoculars show craters along the line between day and night.

Mercury.text: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It never strays far from the Sun in our sky.
Mercury.fact: A year there lasts only 88 Earth days. Look for it low in twilight just after sunset or before sunrise.

Venus.text: A rocky planet covered in thick, bright clouds. After the Moon, it's the brightest natural object in the night sky.
Venus.fact: Binoculars or a small telescope show it going through phases like the Moon.

Earth.text: Our home planet, the only world known to have life.
Earth.fact: The sky view is drawn from your spot on Earth's surface.

Mars.text: A cold desert world that looks orange-red because of rusty dust.
Mars.fact: About every 26 months Earth overtakes Mars, and it becomes much brighter for a few weeks.

Jupiter.text: The largest planet, a giant ball of gas more than 11 times wider than Earth.
Jupiter.fact: Steadily held binoculars show up to four of its moons as tiny dots in a line.

Saturn.text: A gas giant famous for its bright rings of ice.
Saturn.fact: Even a small telescope shows the rings. Their tilt changes over a cycle of about 15 years.

Uranus.text: An ice giant that spins tipped over on its side.
Uranus.fact: Under very dark skies it's just visible without a telescope, but binoculars make it easy to spot as a pale dot.

Neptune.text: The farthest planet: a windy, deep-blue ice giant.
Neptune.fact: It was found in 1846 by working out where it should be, using maths. You need binoculars or a telescope to see it.
